The Python reference

Loading the reference…

90 seconds, one session and four held-out time blocks. A smoke test, not proof of durable predictive performance.

A small research discipline

Keep the future out.

The experiment is only useful if its evaluation is believable.

The question behind BookLab ＋

Can buy and sell pressure help predict the next price move?

Replay a recorded order book, change the prediction horizon and compare a fitted model with simple baselines. The leakage demonstrations show how future information can make a misleading score look convincing.

01

Replay what arrived

The recorded sample contains real historical Coinbase book observations. The other sample is explicitly synthetic. Arrival time determines when information became available.

02

Define one target

Choose a horizon and deadband. The first observation at or after that horizon defines up, unchanged or down. Labels more than 200 ms late or across a session break are discarded.

03

Split, then fit

Use earlier observations for training and validation, and reserve the last period for testing. Training labels that reach into the next period are purged. Scaling learns from training only.

04

Doubt the good result

Compare all three classes and simple baselines. A short-run block interval cannot establish lasting signal. Try the leakage traps, then return to the valid chronological protocol.

What this playground does

It fits browser softmax logistic models, compares validation candidates, refits on development data, and evaluates a held-out period. It runs locally in a worker; no Python server, exchange credentials or live connection is required.

What is still research work

Multiple real days, an exact FI-2010 paper reproduction, independent reruns, costs, fills and execution latency. Prediction scores are not trading profitability.

Welcome to BookLab

Your first experiment.

  1. Play the tape. Scrub through the recorded order book and watch the midpoint.
  2. Change a setting. Try a shorter prediction horizon or remove trailing returns.
  3. Run and compare. Read macro F1, inspect the classes and save the run.

For a useful lesson, open “Try a leakage trap” and give the model the future. The score may improve while the experiment becomes invalid.

Terms of use.

BookLab is an experimental research playground for replaying supplied market samples and comparing prediction models.

Use the results with care

Historical and synthetic examples do not establish future performance. Outputs are educational research results, not investment advice or instructions to place orders. Trading costs, fills and execution latency are not simulated.

Keep the context attached

Check results independently. When sharing them, preserve the sample provenance, method and limitations. Future-target and shuffled-split demonstrations must remain labeled invalid.

About this prototype

The prototype and its samples may change or become unavailable. Third-party data and software remain subject to their respective rights and licences. Please do not attempt to disrupt the service or bypass its access controls.

Last updated · 24 October 2026

Privacy policy.

BookLab’s application runs experiments in your browser. It does not request exchange credentials, payment details or a separate BookLab account, and has no endpoint that uploads your experiment results.

What stays in this browser

When you choose Save experiment, the settings, summary results and save time stay in this browser’s local storage. The Notebook keeps up to 20 runs, without the full prediction list. Remove a run in the Notebook or clear saved experiments in Cookies & storage. Clearing this site’s browser data also removes them.

Your motion choice is stored locally until changed or cleared. Checklist answers last only while this page is open. JSON exports are created locally and stay wherever you choose to save them.

Hosting and access

BookLab includes no advertising or analytics trackers. Images, fonts, scripts and research samples are served with the site. Normal requests still reach the hosting service.

Vercel hosts this version of BookLab. Its handling of technical service data is described in Vercel’s Privacy Policy ↗. Any hosting access controls are managed by Vercel.

For questions about this prototype, contact the person who shared it with you.
